content: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) affects approximately 8% of menstruating women. It is classified as a mood disorder that occurs during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Historically, this condition was referred to as late luteal phase dysphoric disorder. However, in May 1993, the American Psychiatric Association renamed it PMDD in the revised DSM-IV. Initially, PMDD was included in the appendix of the manual as a disorder requiring further study. While many agree that disabling and treatable symptoms should not be ignored, some psychiatrists and women's advocacy groups have expressed concerns about labeling a severe form of premenstrual syndrome (PMS) as a psychiatric disorder. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recognizes PMDD as a legitimate illness. However, it has not been classified as a distinct disorder in the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases (ICD). In 2003, the European Committee for Proprietary Medicinal Products required the manufacturer of Prozac (fluoxetine) to remove PMDD from the list of approved indications for fluoxetine in Europe. The committee concluded that PMDD was not a well-established disease entity across Europe. There was also significant concern that women with less severe premenstrual symptoms might be misdiagnosed with PMDD, leading to inappropriate shortand long-term use of fluoxetine. PMDD is also not included in the Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme. Some commentators have suggested that PMDD, along with other conditions such as social anxiety disorder, restless leg syndrome, and female sexual dysfunction, has been marketed by pharmaceutical companies to increase demand for treatments. However, the marketing of a treatment does not negate the existence of the underlying condition or the genuine distress experienced by sufferers. There is substantial evidence supporting a neurological basis for PMDD. Studies have shown that the self-reported mood symptoms of women with premenstrual dysphoria strongly correlate with a measurable decline in brain serotonin function, as observed through positron emission tomography (PET) scans. Although the exact pathophysiology of PMDD remains unclear, a leading theory attributes the condition to serotonin deficiency, influenced by fluctuations in sex hormone levels (progesterone, estrogen, and testosterone) during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Supporting this theory, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have been shown in clinical trials to effectively treat the mood symptoms of PMDD when administered during the dysphoric phase. PMDD must be differentiated from other conditions, including premenstrual syndrome (PMS), dysmenorrhea, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), and the effects of hormonal therapy. While PMDD shares similarities with PMS, it is more severe and requires treatment because it significantly impairs the individual's ability to function in daily life. The hallmark symptom of PMDD is irritability, which emerges between ovulation and menstruation and resolves within a few days after the onset of bleeding. Other symptoms may include anxiety, anger, depression, mood swings, crying spells, disinterest in daily activities and relationships, difficulty concentrating, fatigue, food cravings or binge eating, sleep disturbances, feelings of being out of control, and physical symptoms such as bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, and joint or muscle pain. Risk factors for PMDD include a history of interpersonal trauma, seasonal changes, sociocultural aspects of female sexual behavior, and stress. Good prognostic factors include the use of oral contraceptives. Lifestyle modifications may help alleviate some symptoms of PMDD. Additionally, certain SSRIs have been approved by the FDA for the treatment of PMDD. Fluoxetine (Prozac) was approved in 2000, sertraline (Zoloft) in 2002, and paroxetine HCl (Paxil) has also received FDA approval. Although the patent for fluoxetine has expired, Eli Lilly obtained a new patent for its use in treating PMDD and marketed it under the trade name Sarafem. However, fluoxetine is now available as a generic medication at a fraction of the cost of branded Sarafem, with the same dosages used for PMDD treatment.
